questions.question: What does SDLC stand for?

options.text: Software Deployment and Launch Cycle
Software Development Lifecycle
System Design and Load Cycle
Software Delivery and Launch Checklist

explanation.correct: SDLC stands for Software Development Lifecycle — the structured process of building software from requirements to monitoring.
explanation.why: A, C, and D are not standard terms. SDLC is a fundamental concept every developer and cloud engineer must know.

questions.question: In the Waterfall model, what happens to requirements once they are gathered?

options.text: They are reviewed every sprint
They are shared with the operations team
They are frozen — no changes allowed
They are documented in Jira

explanation.correct: In Waterfall, requirements are frozen at the start. Going back to change them is extremely expensive and time-consuming.
explanation.why: Waterfall is a linear model — no going back. This is its biggest weakness in real-world projects where requirements evolve.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a problem with the Waterfall methodology?

options.text: Requirements change in real life but cannot be changed
Users get late feedback
The team communicates daily
No partial releases — complete product only at the end

explanation.correct: Daily team communication is a good thing, not a problem. The three major Waterfall problems are frozen requirements, late feedback, and no partial releases.
explanation.why: Waterfall's problems all relate to its rigid, linear structure — not communication patterns.

questions.question: In Agile methodology, what is a sprint?

options.text: A final deployment to production
A short, time-boxed development cycle (typically 1–2 weeks)
A security scan of the codebase
A meeting between the client and operations team

explanation.correct: A sprint is a short, time-boxed iteration (usually 1–2 weeks) in which the team plans, builds, and delivers a working increment of software.
explanation.why: Sprints are the core unit of Agile work. Everything else — planning, review, retrospective — happens in relation to a sprint.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of Jira in an Agile project?

options.text: Deploy code to production
Monitor server performance
Plan, assign, track, and report work in sprints
Store built application packages

explanation.correct: Jira is a project management tool for organizing work — writing user stories, assigning tasks, tracking status (To Do / In Progress / Done).
explanation.why: Jira is not a deployment or monitoring tool. It is purely for planning and tracking sprint work.

questions.question: What does the 'Works on My Laptop' problem describe?

options.text: A developer's laptop is too slow for coding
Code works in the developer's environment but fails in production due to configuration differences
The application deploys too slowly
The CI pipeline fails to trigger

explanation.correct: This describes the environment mismatch problem — different OS, software versions, or configurations between developer machines and production servers.
explanation.why: This is one of the two core problems DevOps solves. The fix is standardizing environments using Docker containers.

questions.question: What is the main difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?

options.text: Continuous Delivery skips testing; Continuous Deployment includes it
Continuous Delivery requires manual approval before production; Continuous Deployment deploys automatically
Continuous Delivery deploys to staging only; Continuous Deployment deploys to dev only
They are the same thing with different names

explanation.correct: Continuous Delivery keeps the package ready and waits for a human to click approve before pushing to production. Continuous Deployment automatically deploys when all tests pass.
explanation.why: This is a very common exam question. The key word is 'manual approval' — present in Delivery, absent in Deployment.

questions.question: What is the role of SonarQube in a CI/CD pipeline?

options.text: Build and compile source code
Store versioned deployment packages
Scan code for quality issues, security vulnerabilities, and test coverage
Run the application on production servers

explanation.correct: SonarQube performs static code analysis — it reads source code without running it and flags bugs, vulnerabilities, code smells, and coverage gaps.
explanation.why: SonarQube is placed after the build and test steps, acting as a quality gate before the artifact is stored or deployed.

questions.question: What does Jenkins do in a CI/CD pipeline?

options.text: It compiles the source code into executable binaries
It stores all built application packages
It orchestrates and connects all tools in the pipeline
It monitors application performance in production

explanation.correct: Jenkins is an orchestration tool — it connects and coordinates Maven, JUnit, SonarQube, JFrog, and deployment steps into a single automated workflow.
explanation.why: Jenkins is often called the 'conductor of the orchestra.' It does not build or test code itself — it tells other tools when and how to run.

questions.question: What does Maven do in a CI/CD pipeline?

options.text: Runs unit tests on individual functions
Compiles and packages source code with its dependencies
Scans code for security vulnerabilities
Stores deployment artifacts with version numbers

explanation.correct: Maven is a build tool for Java applications. It compiles source code and bundles all dependencies into a deployable package (JAR/WAR file).
explanation.why: Without Maven (or a similar build tool), source code is just text — it cannot run on a server.

questions.question: A developer pushes code to the main branch. The Jenkins pipeline runs and the SonarQube quality gate fails. What happens next?

options.text: The code is automatically deployed to production with a warning
The pipeline stops and notifies the development team to fix the issue
The code is rolled back to the previous version automatically
Jenkins retries the SonarQube scan three times before failing

explanation.correct: When a quality gate fails, the CI/CD pipeline stops immediately. The development team receives a notification (via Jenkins dashboard or Slack integration) and must fix the issues before the pipeline can proceed.
explanation.why: This is the core value of CI — catching problems early, before code reaches production. Stopping the pipeline prevents bad code from being deployed.

questions.question: Your team uses Agile with 2-week sprints but deploys manually at the end of each sprint. The operations team often delays releases, saying deployment is risky. What is the BEST solution?

options.text: Switch back to Waterfall to reduce deployment frequency
Have developers deploy directly, bypassing the operations team
Implement a CI/CD pipeline to automate testing and deployment with Continuous Delivery
Increase sprint length to 4 weeks to reduce deployment frequency

explanation.correct: A CI/CD pipeline automates testing and gives the operations team verifiable test reports and a one-click controlled deployment. Continuous Delivery (not full Deployment) is best first because it maintains human approval while removing manual deployment steps.
explanation.why: The real problem is that manual deployment feels risky because there are no automated checks. CI/CD provides those checks and builds trust.

questions.question: What is JFrog Artifactory used for in a CI/CD pipeline?

options.text: Running automated unit tests
Scanning code for security vulnerabilities
Storing and versioning built deployment packages
Monitoring production server health

explanation.correct: JFrog Artifactory is an artifact repository. Every successful build produces a versioned artifact stored in JFrog. This enables rollback to any previous version if a deployment fails.
explanation.why: Without versioned artifact storage, you have no reliable way to roll back to a known-good version of the application.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the relationship between Agile and DevOps?

options.text: Agile and DevOps are competing methodologies — you choose one or the other
Agile defines what to build each sprint; DevOps defines how to build, test, and deploy it
DevOps replaces Agile in modern software development
Agile is used by developers; DevOps is used only by operations teams

explanation.correct: Agile and DevOps are complementary. Agile handles planning and flexible requirements. DevOps handles automation, deployment, and reliable operations. They work together, not against each other.
explanation.why: A common misconception is that DevOps replaces Agile. In practice, most companies use both simultaneously.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a feature branch in a DevOps workflow?

options.text: A branch used only by the operations team for deployment
A dedicated branch where developers write and test their own code before merging to main
A branch that stores production artifacts
A branch used exclusively for hotfixes

explanation.correct: Developers work in feature branches to isolate their changes from the main codebase. When their feature is ready and tested, they create a pull request to merge into the main branch, which triggers the CI/CD pipeline.
explanation.why: Working directly in the main branch would mean every developer's untested code immediately affects the entire team. Feature branches provide safe isolation.

questions.question: What is Infrastructure as Code (IaC)?

options.text: Writing application code that runs on infrastructure
Managing cloud infrastructure — servers, networks, databases — using code files instead of manual console clicks
Storing code files on cloud storage services
Writing automated unit tests for infrastructure components

explanation.correct: IaC means describing your cloud infrastructure (VPCs, EC2 instances, databases) in code files. Tools like Terraform read these files and create the infrastructure automatically, consistently, and repeatably.
explanation.why: IaC eliminates environment mismatch and manual setup errors by ensuring Dev, Staging, and Production environments are created from the same code.

questions.question: What is the difference between Terraform and Ansible?

options.text: Terraform is for AWS only; Ansible works on any cloud
Terraform provisions infrastructure; Ansible manages software configuration on servers
Terraform is open source; Ansible requires a paid license
Terraform manages databases; Ansible manages networking

explanation.correct: Terraform creates and manages infrastructure (the server, network, database). Ansible configures what's ON the server — installing packages, updating software, managing configuration files.
explanation.why: Both are IaC tools but with different responsibilities. In a complete DevOps setup, Terraform provisions the servers and Ansible configures them.

questions.question: In a CI/CD pipeline, what is a Quality Gate?

options.text: A physical security checkpoint at the data center
The server that receives production deployments
An automated checkpoint that stops the pipeline if code quality metrics fall below defined thresholds
A manual review step where managers approve code

explanation.correct: A Quality Gate is configured in the pipeline (often in SonarQube integrated with Jenkins). If code coverage is below 80% or there are critical security vulnerabilities, the gate blocks deployment automatically.
explanation.why: Quality Gates make quality enforcement automatic and objective — no human needs to remember to check coverage or security every time.

questions.question: A sprint ends on Friday. The development team has merged all features. The CI/CD pipeline has passed all stages. The package is sitting in JFrog. Nothing has been deployed to production yet. Which CD practice is this?

options.text: Continuous Deployment — because deployment happened automatically
Continuous Delivery — because the package is ready but awaiting manual approval to go live
Continuous Integration — because all tests passed
None — this describes Waterfall delivery

explanation.correct: Continuous Delivery means the code is always in a deployable state — tested, built, packaged — but a human decides when to actually push it to production. The pipeline stops before the final deploy step.
explanation.why: If the pipeline had automatically deployed to production when tests passed, that would be Continuous Deployment. The key differentiator is whether a human approval is required.

questions.question: Why does manual deployment cause websites to go down during Agile sprints?

options.text: The developers delete the database during deployment
The operations team must stop the application, copy new files, change configuration, and restart — all while the server is unavailable
AWS automatically shuts down EC2 instances during updates
CI/CD pipelines require the website to be offline during scanning

explanation.correct: Manual deployment involves multiple sequential steps: stop app → copy files → update config → restart. During these steps, the application is not running. This downtime affects real users, which is why operations teams resist frequent deployments.
explanation.why: CI/CD pipelines solve this with blue-green deployments and rolling updates that can deploy new versions with zero or near-zero downtime.

questions.question: A company runs a banking application. They want to deploy updates automatically whenever code passes all tests, but they are concerned about regulatory requirements that mandate a human sign-off before any production change. Which approach should they use?

options.text: Continuous Deployment — because banking needs speed
Waterfall — because banking cannot use automation
Continuous Delivery — which keeps deployments automated but requires human approval before production
No CI/CD — banking applications should be deployed manually only

explanation.correct: Continuous Delivery is the correct choice. It automates all testing and packaging stages, and makes the application always ready to deploy — but it holds for human approval before the production push. This satisfies regulatory change-approval requirements.
explanation.why: Most financial and healthcare organizations use Continuous Delivery rather than Continuous Deployment precisely because their compliance frameworks require human sign-off on production changes.

questions.question: Your CI/CD pipeline deploys a new version to production. Within 5 minutes, monitoring shows a spike in 500 errors. What is the FASTEST recovery action assuming JFrog Artifactory is in use?

options.text: Wait for developers to fix the bug and push a new version
Roll back to the previous artifact version stored in JFrog and redeploy
Disable the affected feature flags in the application
Terminate the EC2 instance and launch a new one

explanation.correct: With JFrog Artifactory storing all versioned artifacts, rolling back means selecting the previous version and triggering a redeployment — often a one-click or single pipeline run. This is far faster than writing and deploying a fix.
explanation.why: This is the core value of artifact versioning. Without it, rollback requires rebuilding the old code from scratch — which may take 20–30 minutes or more under pressure.

questions.question: A developer argues that since their team uses feature branches, they don't need Continuous Integration because their main branch is always clean. What is wrong with this reasoning?

options.text: Nothing — feature branches make CI unnecessary
Feature branches can diverge significantly from main; CI catches integration bugs when branches merge, which cannot be caught in isolated branch testing
Feature branches cannot be used with CI/CD pipelines
CI runs only on the main branch, so feature branches are irrelevant

explanation.correct: Feature branches can drift far from the main branch over days or weeks. When two developers merge their branches simultaneously, the combined code may break even if each branch tested perfectly in isolation. CI catches these integration failures immediately at merge time.
explanation.why: This is called an 'integration bug' — individual components work but break when combined. CI's value is precisely in catching these at the earliest possible moment.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why DevOps culture emphasizes 'shared responsibility' between Dev and Ops?

options.text: To reduce the number of employees needed in both teams
To ensure both teams use the same programming language
To eliminate the blame game and ensure both teams are accountable for quality, reliability, and speed of delivery
To make developers responsible for all server administration tasks

explanation.correct: In traditional development, Dev's goal was to write features fast, Ops' goal was to keep production stable. These incentives conflicted, causing the blame game. Shared responsibility means both teams are measured on the same outcomes — delivery speed AND reliability.
explanation.why: This is the cultural core of DevOps. Tools like CI/CD pipelines make shared responsibility practical — both teams see the same test reports, the same deployment logs, and the same production metrics.

questions.question: In a DevOps pipeline, after code passes SonarQube analysis, the artifact is stored in JFrog and then deployed to a staging environment. Before promoting to production, what should happen?

options.text: Developers manually review all 10,000 lines of changed code
The artifact is rebuilt from source code again for security
Integration testing, QA sign-off, and any required manual approvals are completed
The staging servers are terminated to save cost before production deployment

explanation.correct: Staging is a pre-production environment that mirrors production. After deployment to staging, QA runs integration and end-to-end tests. Once these pass and appropriate approvals are obtained, the same artifact (not rebuilt) is promoted to production.
explanation.why: Notice: the artifact is NOT rebuilt for production. The same verified artifact from JFrog moves through environments. Rebuilding would introduce risk — the production build might differ from the tested build.

questions.question: What problem does having multiple SDLC environments (Dev, Staging, Production) with identical configurations solve?

options.text: It reduces the number of developers needed
It allows teams to test changes in conditions identical to production before customers are affected
It ensures production runs faster than staging
It allows different teams to use different programming languages

explanation.correct: Identical environments ensure that if code works in Staging, it will work in Production — because both have the same OS, same software versions, same configurations. The only difference is resource capacity.
explanation.why: This directly addresses the 'works on my laptop' problem — when environments are standardized and identical, environment-specific failures are eliminated.

questions.question: A team decides to implement Continuous Deployment. What is the MINIMUM requirement for this to be safe?

options.text: At least 3 developers on the team
A comprehensive automated test suite that validates both functionality and security before deployment
A dedicated operations team to monitor production after each deployment
A rollback plan documented in a Word document

explanation.correct: Continuous Deployment removes human approval entirely. The only safety net is the automated test suite. If tests are incomplete or low quality, bad code can reach production automatically. High test coverage with unit, integration, and security tests is the prerequisite.
explanation.why: This is why many teams start with Continuous Delivery first — to build confidence in their test suite — before advancing to full Continuous Deployment.

questions.question: What is the purpose of JaCoCo in a CI/CD pipeline?

options.text: It orchestrates the entire pipeline and connects all tools
It measures what percentage of source code lines are exercised by automated tests
It stores deployment artifacts with version numbers
It provisions cloud infrastructure for test environments

explanation.correct: JaCoCo (Java Code Coverage) measures code coverage — what percentage of your source code is actually executed when your test suite runs. This metric is fed into SonarQube as part of the quality gate analysis.
explanation.why: High code coverage does not guarantee bug-free code, but low coverage means large portions of your codebase are untested and could hide defects.

questions.question: Which scenario describes a correctly implemented CI/CD pipeline?

options.text: Developer pushes code → Manual testing for 2 days → Manual deployment every 3 months
Developer pushes code → Pipeline triggers automatically → Tests run → Quality gate checks → Artifact stored → Auto-deployed or manual approval → Monitoring
Developer pushes code → Jenkins sends code to production directly without testing
Developer pushes code → Operations team manually runs each pipeline stage

explanation.correct: A correctly implemented CI/CD pipeline is fully automated from code push to deployment, with quality gates at each stage and monitoring after deployment. Human involvement is limited to reviewing reports and optionally approving the production release.
explanation.why: Options A and D describe manual processes. Option C skips quality gates entirely. Only B shows the complete automated pipeline with appropriate quality controls.

questions.question: A company switches from Waterfall to Agile + DevOps. Which of the following outcomes would they most likely see?

options.text: Fewer deployments per year and more stable releases
More frequent releases, earlier bug detection, reduced deployment risk, and faster customer feedback
Increased manual testing effort and more operations staff required
Higher project cost due to automation tooling, with no improvement in speed

explanation.correct: Agile + DevOps enables more frequent, smaller releases (reducing risk per release), automated testing catches bugs earlier (before production), CI/CD reduces manual effort, and customers provide feedback on real features sooner.
explanation.why: This is the fundamental value proposition of Agile + DevOps. The combined approach directly addresses all three Waterfall problems: slow delivery, frozen requirements, and late feedback.
